scoreNote: Strong (5): agrees that welfare is the better indicator because it is representative of the whole nation, cannot be faked, and tends to underlie achievement, while granting that great achievements remain a real and related sign of greatness.

sentences.text: Confronted with two nations — one of glittering monuments and miserable masses, the other of modest art but healthy, free, and educated citizens — which would we call the greater?
The claim answers without hesitation, holding that the general welfare of a nation's people is a better indication of its greatness than the achievements of its rulers, artists, or scientists.

The claim is right: welfare is the better indicator because it is more representative, harder to fake, and more durable than achievement, even though great achievements remain a real and related sign of a nation's strength.
Welfare is the better indicator first because it represents the whole nation rather than a fraction of it.
The achievements of rulers, artists, and scientists are the work of a tiny, gifted elite, and they tell us what a nation's best can do, not how its ordinary people live.
A nation can produce world-famous artists while most of its people go hungry, so its celebrated art tells us little about the condition of the many.
General welfare, by contrast, is a measure of the entire population, sampling the whole rather than its rare peaks, and so it indicates the state of the nation far more faithfully.
Because it speaks for everyone and not just the gifted few, welfare is the more representative measure.
Furthermore, welfare is the better indicator because it cannot be counterfeited.
A repressive or deeply unequal regime can still fund a few brilliant artists or scientists and parade them as proof of greatness, masking the suffering beneath.
But the broad health, freedom, and prosperity of an entire population cannot be staged for show, since either the many live well or they plainly do not.
Achievement can be a glittering surface laid over a rotten foundation, whereas widespread welfare is the foundation itself, visible to anyone who looks.
Greatness that can be faked by a handful of names is no sure greatness; welfare, which cannot, is the truer test.

sections.role: Body — Achievement is related, not opposed

sentences.text: Still, the claim need not despise achievement, for the two are not enemies.
Great achievements are a genuine sign of a nation's vitality, and a people who are healthy, free, and educated will tend to produce more of them.
The point is not that achievements are worthless, but that they are a partial and unreliable indicator, while welfare is comprehensive and dependable.
Where welfare is high, achievement usually follows; where achievement is high but welfare low, we should suspect a greatness that serves the few at the expense of the many.
Welfare is the better indicator precisely because it captures what achievement alone can hide.
In conclusion, the claim is sound: the general welfare of a nation's people indicates its greatness better than the achievements of its rulers, artists, or scientists.

Welfare measures the whole nation rather than a gifted fraction, it cannot be faked as a few celebrated achievements can, and it tends to be the very ground from which real achievement grows, so it is the fuller and more honest sign of greatness.
Read a nation's greatness in the lives of its many, not the names of its few.
